name: How to Plan Your Perfect Kitchen Layout

step.name: Step 1: Document Your Current Space and Lifestyle
step.text: Take detailed measurements of your existing kitchen. Crucially, reflect on how you *actually* use your kitchen: where do you prep, cook, and clean? What frustrates you most? Consider your household's unique needs, whether it's a bustling family hub or a quiet space for two.

step.name: Step 2: Define Your Needs and Wishes for the New Layout
step.text: Think about your storage requirements, desired appliance types and sizes, and how many people typically use the kitchen at once. Do you dream of a kitchen island, more counter space, or a dedicated pantry? This helps a professional understand your vision and translate it into a practical design.

step.name: Step 3: Consider the Work Triangle and Traffic Paths
step.text: The National Kitchen and Bath Association (NKBA) recommends a work triangle (sink, cooktop, refrigerator) with legs between 4–9 feet, totaling no more than 26 feet, without major traffic crossing it. Map out how people will move through the space to ensure smooth flow and prevent bottlenecks, especially around high-use areas.

step.name: Step 4: Develop Layout Alternatives with Professional Help
step.text: This is where a residential design-build team shines. They can provide CAD-supported layouts, showing you various options for appliance placement, cabinet configurations, and overall flow. This visual guidance is invaluable for making informed decisions before any physical work begins, coordinating everything from plumbing to electrical.

step.name: Step 5: Confirm Appliance Dimensions and Utility Locations
step.text: Once you have a preferred layout, verify the exact dimensions of all new appliances to ensure they fit perfectly. Coordinate with your design-build team to review existing plumbing, electrical, and ventilation locations, understanding what can remain and what needs to be moved or upgraded. This prevents costly surprises later and ensures a managed process.

step.name: Step 6: Plan for Permits and Inspections
step.text: Changes to plumbing, electrical, gas, or structural elements often require permits. Your design-build contractor will handle permit coordination, which can add 1–6 weeks to the timeline. Account for this in your schedule and understand that various inspections will occur throughout the construction phase to ensure everything meets local building codes in the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex.
